log_retention.title: Log Retention and Review
log_retention.hint: Audit data retention and daily review (PCI 10.4.1/10.5.1). Since the checkpoint chain was enabled, audit logs are purged by checkpoint interval: if any row in an interval has not expired, the whole interval is retained, so a few already-expired rows may remain after the first purge (expected behavior, not a defect). Checkpoint retention defaults to 0 (forever) and must not be shorter than the longest of the four data retention keys (0 means forever): the proof must outlive the data it proves, and violating batches are rejected in full.

access_policy.title: Connection Policy
access_policy.hint: The global default decides whether assets without an individual policy require a request before connecting (PCI Req 7.2 least privilege); each asset can override it in the table below or in the asset form. Administrators are exempt from requests (each connection leaves an audit marker)

request_params.title: Access Request Parameters
request_params.hint: Request duration cap and pending timeout (PCI Req 7.2). Minimum approvals is an internal-control hardening option (dual-review convention, not a PCI requirement): at 2 or more, a request only takes effect after distinct approvers approve it up to the threshold; if the threshold exceeds an asset's available approvers, the request needs admin backfill or times out

break_glass.title: Break-Glass and Revocation
break_glass.hint: Break-glass lets someone with connection authorization connect first and be reviewed afterwards when no approver is available (off by default; when off, admins can still connect on a user's behalf in emergencies). Revoke-disconnect decides whether revoking a timed authorization early also interrupts ongoing sessions (default blocks new connections only)

transport.title: Transmission Security Policy
transport.hint: Enforcement ladder for six transport channels (PCI Req 4): Unrestricted = no impact / Warn and Record = connection consent or archive confirmation goes to the audit log / Strictly Reject = asset transmission settings must be completed first (see the channel inventory precheck below for affected counts); the LDAP fix is on the Directory (LDAP) page (change the directory address to ldaps://)

key.title: Key Management Policy
key.hint: Key rotation reminder (cryptoperiod, in the spirit of PCI 3.7.4); reminder only, triggers no action

data_transfer.title: Data Transfer Control
data_transfer.hint: Controls whether data can move in or out of managed assets. The two clipboard keys are enforced only for graphical protocols (RDP/VNC) and take effect on the next connection. The three file keys apply immediately to SFTP file management, graphical-channel file transfer and K8s container file transfer. Copy/paste in text terminals (SSH / database CLI / K8s exec) happens inside the browser and cannot be enforced by the server; carrying data out via shell commands is handled by command blocking, not by this section

cluster.title: Cluster access
cluster.hint: How many seconds to wait for data from a Kubernetes cluster. Set it too low and healthy clusters look unreachable. This is only a wait time — it does not affect who can access what.

offsite.title: Local copies
offsite.hint: Once offsite storage is on, local recording copies can be removed early to save disk; recordings still play back from the offsite copy. This setting has no effect while the feature is off.

transferBoundary.title: Control boundaries of this section (expand to read)
transferBoundary.item1: Clipboard policy is enforceable only for graphical protocols (RDP/VNC). Copy and paste in SSH, database CLI and K8s exec happen inside the browser, where the server cannot tell a paste from keystrokes; hiding buttons in the UI is an interface constraint, not a control.
transferBoundary.item2: Clipboard enforcement happens inside guacd, so this product never sees the blocked attempt and clipboard denials produce no audit event. File transfer denials do produce a denied audit record.
transferBoundary.item3: Session share viewers inherit the connection parameters of the session and are not evaluated against their own grants: a user allowed to paste who shares the session lets the viewer paste too.
transferBoundary.item4: K8s file endpoints currently check only the asset update permission, bypassing connect authorization and access policy tiers. This section adds only the data transfer check.
transferBoundary.item5: Data taken out from inside a terminal via scp, curl or base64 is out of scope here and belongs to command blocking: disabling file download does not mean data cannot leave.
transferBoundary.item6: A blocked download on the graphical channel is discarded silently: the client receives no error response and simply sees nothing happen. A blocked upload does get an explicit rejection.
transferBoundary.item7: The result grid of the database query console is rendered in the browser and can be selected, copied or read with developer tools; there is no server-side enforcement point. The only thing these keys govern is the export endpoint, the single controlled exit for results.

policyNote.audit_checkpoint_interval_seconds: Whichever of the two thresholds is reached first triggers sealing. Only records that have been sealed are protected by the chain: if a record created between the last sealing and the next is deleted outright, sealing captures the state after the deletion and it cannot be discovered afterwards from local data. A shorter interval narrows that window, a longer one widens it; outright deletion has to be carried by the off-box copy held on the external log collector. The maximum is 86400 seconds (24 hours), and it cannot be set to 0, because sealing must not be effectively turned off.
policyNote.audit_checkpoint_row_threshold: Whichever of the two thresholds is reached first triggers sealing. Only records that have been sealed are protected by the chain: once this many records have accumulated, sealing happens early rather than waiting out the full interval, so the window does not widen during busy periods. A lower value narrows that window, a higher one widens it; if a record in the window is deleted outright, sealing captures the state after the deletion and it cannot be discovered afterwards from local data, so that risk is carried by the off-box copy held on the external log collector. The maximum is 1000000 records, and it cannot be set to 0, because sealing must not be effectively turned off.
policyNote.audit_chain_recent_verify_days: When the system observes that a new sealing has completed, it re-verifies the contents of sealed intervals from the last N days (at most once per sealing interval), so tampering near the end of the chain surfaces without waiting for the full-chain rotation to reach it. A shorter window costs less per run and covers fewer intervals; a longer one covers more but takes longer each time, and beyond 30 days its coverage already overlaps full-chain verification, so all that is added is cost. The window covers sealed intervals only — records not yet sealed are not included, and that window is carried by the checkpoint sealing interval — and the days actually applied are the lesser of this value and the audit log retention period, because records outside retention have already been removed by policy and promising to verify them would be an empty promise. The maximum is 30 days and it cannot be set to 0; at the minimum of 1 day the window still contains the newest interval, so the mechanism never drops to nothing. The guarantee that all history is eventually re-verified is carried by the full-chain verification interval and the scan rate; raising this value is not a substitute for them. Changing this value changes what this system states to auditors ("the last N days are re-verified automatically after sealing").
policyNote.audit_chain_verify_interval_seconds: At this interval the system verifies the whole checkpoint chain: the structural layer checks continuity and signatures across the chain, while the content layer advances through a slice of history at the configured scan rate. A shorter interval surfaces anomalies sooner and keeps each run small; a longer one scales each run up proportionally and delays detection in this layer — but the time needed to work through all history stays the same, because what each run scans is the scan rate multiplied by this interval. This verification does not cover records that have not been sealed yet; that window is carried by the checkpoint sealing interval, and outright deletion still has to be carried by the off-box copy held on the external log collector. The maximum is 604800 seconds (7 days) and it cannot be set to 0, because automatic verification must not be effectively turned off; a single run costs only seconds, so there is no operational reason to make it sparser. Changing this value changes what this system states to auditors ("the whole chain is verified automatically every X").
policyNote.audit_chain_verify_rows_per_hour: The content layer re-reads the records in sealed intervals and checks them against what was recorded when the interval was sealed, advancing at this rate: the entries actually scanned per run are this rate multiplied by the full-chain verification interval, so changing that interval does not change how long it takes to work through all history — only how long each run takes. This content verification covers sealed intervals only — records not yet sealed are not included, and that window is carried by the checkpoint sealing interval. A higher rate completes a pass sooner at a higher load on the database; a lower one takes longer, and once a pass takes longer than the retention period, old intervals are removed before their turn ever comes and content verification of that stretch of history effectively never runs. The minimum of 10000 entries/hour sits exactly at that point (on a fully loaded ten-year chain a pass takes about ten years). The minimum only blocks "turned down so far it is effectively off"; it does not decide the throttling preference for the administrator, who still chooses freely between 10000 and 5000000. The maximum is 5000000 entries/hour (beyond that the load on a production database is more than it can carry), and it cannot be set to 0, because scanning must not be effectively turned off. Changing this value changes what this system states to auditors ("all history is re-verified roughly every Y days").
policyNote.retention_max_per_run: The retention policy removes data past its retention period daily. This value caps how many records each run may delete per data class, so no single run overloads the database. Raise it to clear more per run, which is what lets cleanup catch up when data volume is high or a retention period was just shortened; lower it to ease database load, at the cost of expired data accumulating. If data arrives faster than it is cleared, expired data stays indefinitely while the screen still reports daily cleanup. A 5,000-record floor applies because that is one batch: below it a run cannot finish even a single batch, so the clearing rate falls below the arrival rate of any real deployment — under this value the mechanism stops working rather than merely running slower. Whatever is left is marked incomplete and resumes the next day.
policyNote.key_rotation_max_per_run: When the data encryption key is replaced, existing encrypted data must be re-encrypted record by record. This value caps how many records each run processes, controlling how long one operation takes. Unprocessed records keep their progress, and running again resumes from there. Raise it to process more per run and finish sooner overall, at the cost of longer individual runs; lower it for shorter runs that need more repetitions. Set too low, key replacement can never actually finish, while the key inventory still offers replacement. A 500-record floor applies because that is one read unit: below it a single operation makes no progress at all — under this value the mechanism stops working. Reading existing data is unaffected throughout.
policyNote.k8s_list_timeout_seconds: When picking a container, this is how long to wait for the cluster's list of running items. Time out and you get an error. Higher: busy or distant clusters get more time, but a real outage takes longer to surface. Lower: outages surface faster, but healthy clusters may be misjudged. Floor is 3s — a single query can spend a second or two just setting up the encrypted connection; below that even healthy clusters all become unreachable while still listed among your assets.

keyManagement.description: Envelope encryption key inventory and rekey wizard; all rotations are manual and the system never rotates keys automatically
keyManagement.rewrapPendingTitle: KEK rewrap not yet switched over
keyManagement.rewrapPendingDesc: The new KEK has been rewrapped and persisted, but the service is still running on the old KEK. Store the new KEK you entered in the wizard into the ENCRYPTION_KEY environment variable and restart the service to complete the switch; everything works as usual until then, and key rotation is temporarily disabled (restored after the switch).
keyManagement.rewrapPendingDescUi: The new KEK has been rewrapped and persisted, but the service is still running on the old KEK. This deployment runs in ui mode: restart the backend service, then enter the new KEK you entered in the wizard on the unseal page to complete the switch. Do not write it into .env or ENCRYPTION_KEY. Everything works as usual until then, and key rotation is temporarily disabled (restored after the switch).
keyManagement.rewrapPendingDescDelegated: The new KEK has been rewrapped and persisted, but the service is still running on the old KEK. This deployment's KEK is held by a delegated provider, so completing the switchover is a deployment-level provider migration — follow section 4 of the operations runbook docs/ops/privileged-credential-rotation.md. Everything works as usual until then, and key rotation is temporarily disabled (restored after the switch).
keyManagement.rewrapPendingDescUnknown: The new KEK has been rewrapped and persisted, but the service is still running on the old KEK. How to complete the switch depends on this deployment's KEK_PROVIDER (env: write it into ENCRYPTION_KEY and restart; ui: restart and enter it on the unseal page — do not write it into .env; kms / hsm: follow the operations runbook) — confirm the mode before acting. Everything works as usual until then, and key rotation is temporarily disabled (restored after the switch).
keyManagement.abandonRewrapConfirm: This marks the not-yet-switched new-KEK wrapping rows as retired (material is retained and can later be destroyed via "Clean up retired data") and returns to the pre-rewrap state — the service keeps running on the current KEK and existing data stays decryptable. Safe to abandon if you lost the new KEK or decided not to switch. Abandon this switch?
keyManagement.rotationPendingDesc: {n} records have not yet been re-encrypted to the current version (still readable). Click "Rotate data encryption key (DEK)" below again to resume with the current version; no new version is created.
keyManagement.cryptoperiodDesc: {keys} have exceeded the reminder period ({days} days). This is only a reminder and triggers no action; rotate them at your convenience using the wizard below.
keyManagement.systemKeysHint: Generated by the system and stored in the database wrapped by the KEK; retired versions are kept permanently to decrypt old data and verify historical seals
keyManagement.envKeysHint: Stored in environment variables; the product cannot rotate them programmatically—see the key runbook in the deployment baseline docs for rotation steps
keyManagement.rewrapIntro1: A KEK (master key) rewrap re-wraps all system keys with the new master key you supply, {emphasis} (completes in seconds).
keyManagement.rewrapIntro2: Process: you enter or locally generate the new KEK → the system re-wraps with it → you store the new KEK in the {code} environment variable → restart the service to complete the switch. Until the switch is done, the service keeps running on the current KEK and will not lock up.
keyManagement.rewrapIntro2Ui: Process: you enter or locally generate the new KEK → the system re-wraps with it → you restart the backend service → you enter that new KEK on the unseal page, which completes the switch. This deployment runs in ui mode (the key material lives only in memory): do not write the new KEK into {dotenv} or the {code} environment variable. Until the switch is done, the service keeps running on the current KEK and will not lock up.
keyManagement.rewrapIntro2Delegated: Process: you enter or locally generate the new KEK → the system re-wraps with it → you make the new KEK effective following your deployment procedure. This deployment's KEK is held by a delegated provider ({mode}) and this wizard only offers a local KEK target, so completing the switch amounts to a deployment-level migration from the delegated mode back to a local mode — follow the operations runbook for the steps. Until the switch is done, the service keeps running on the current KEK and will not lock up.
keyManagement.rewrapIntro2Unknown: Process: you enter or locally generate the new KEK → the system re-wraps with it → the new KEK enters the backend process to complete the switch. The KEK mode of this deployment cannot be confirmed right now (the inventory has not loaded, or reported no provider), and the last step differs per mode: confirm the deployment's KEK_PROVIDER first — the final step of this wizard lists what to do for each mode. Until the switch is done, the service keeps running on the current KEK and will not lock up.
keyManagement.kekOnceTitle: The new KEK exists only in your hands
keyManagement.kekOnceDesc: The server never generates, returns, persists, or logs the new KEK — you supply it or generate it locally, and the system only reports its fingerprint and the number of rewrapped keys. Prepare a secure storage location (deployment secret management) before continuing.
keyManagement.kekSaveNowDesc: The material is cleared from this screen once submitted, and the system has no way to show it again. Losing the new KEK after the switchover makes existing data permanently undecryptable.
keyManagement.kekInputPlaceholder: 32 chars, 64 hex, or base64 decoding to 32 bytes
keyManagement.kekFormatHint: The new KEK is a 32-byte key. Three forms are accepted: 32 characters (A-Z a-z 0-9), 64 hexadecimal characters, or base64 that decodes to exactly 32 bytes. This check is an input aid; acceptance is always decided by server-side validation — the server additionally rejects the factory default value and keys matching the current or any previously used key, which this browser cannot determine.
keyManagement.kekErrorCharset: When entering the key as 32 characters directly, only A-Z a-z 0-9 are allowed; to use other bytes, enter the key in hexadecimal or base64 instead
keyManagement.kekSameAsCurrent: Same fingerprint as the current KEK: the rewrap target must be a different key
keyManagement.kekConfirmPlaceholder: Enter it again; both fields must match exactly
keyManagement.kekConfirmMismatch: The two entries differ: please confirm before submitting
keyManagement.kekConfirmHint: An exact match between the two fields is the only mechanical precondition the server trusts for accepting a rewrap; the server performs the same comparison independently.
keyManagement.kekGenerateFailed: Cannot generate a KEK locally: this browser does not provide crypto.getRandomValues
keyManagement.kekSavedCheckbox: I have saved the new KEK to a secure location and understand that losing it makes existing data permanently undecryptable
keyManagement.finalStepsIntro: Final two steps (run on the deployment host):
keyManagement.finalStep1: Change the {env} environment variable to the new KEK you just saved (for docker-compose deployments, edit {dotenv} or the compose file).
keyManagement.finalStep2: Restart the backend service. On startup, after the system verifies the new KEK can unwrap all keys, it marks the old wrapping rows as retired and completes the switch (material is retained until you run explicit cleanup from the inventory).
keyManagement.finalNote: Until completion, this page shows the "KEK rewrap not yet switched over" reminder; the service keeps running on the old KEK. If you decide to abandon the switch, re-run the rewrap wizard to void this new KEK.
keyManagement.finalStepsIntroUi: Final two steps (this deployment runs in ui mode):
keyManagement.finalStep1Ui: Restart the backend service. In ui mode the service returns to the sealed state after a restart and stops serving until someone unseals it.
keyManagement.finalStep2Ui: Enter the new KEK you just saved on the unseal page. During unseal, after the system verifies the new KEK can unwrap all keys, it marks the old wrapping rows as retired and completes the switchover (material is retained until you run explicit cleanup from the inventory).
keyManagement.uiNoEnvTitle: Do not write the new KEK into .env or any environment variable
keyManagement.uiNoEnvDesc: This deployment runs in ui mode: the KEK material lives only in memory and never touches disk — that is the only protection this mode provides. Writing the new KEK into .env or ENCRYPTION_KEY would leave the root key in plaintext on disk. The new KEK is entered on the unseal page only.
keyManagement.finalStepsIntroDelegated: This deployment's KEK is held by a delegated provider ({mode}); completing the switchover is a deployment-level provider migration:
keyManagement.finalStepsDelegatedBody: Two things are confirmed: this wizard only offers a local KEK target, so this rewrap produced local material; and migrating from a delegated mode back to a local mode must go through a rewrap (now done). The remaining steps involve changing the KEK_PROVIDER declaration and the cloud key configuration, which is not settled inside the product — follow section 4 of the operations runbook docs/ops/privileged-credential-rotation.md and your own cloud key procedures. This page does not give step-by-step instructions, so as not to state steps that have not been verified.
keyManagement.finalStepsIntroUnknown: The KEK mode of this deployment cannot be confirmed (the inventory has not loaded, or reported no provider). Choose the steps that match the deployment's KEK_PROVIDER:
keyManagement.finalStepUnknownEnv: env mode: change the ENCRYPTION_KEY environment variable to the new KEK you just saved (for docker-compose deployments, edit .env or the compose file), then restart the backend service; the switch completes on startup.
keyManagement.finalStepUnknownUi: ui mode: restart the backend service, then enter the new KEK you just saved on the unseal page; the switch completes during unseal. Do not write the new KEK into .env or ENCRYPTION_KEY — in ui mode the key material never touches disk.
keyManagement.finalStepUnknownDelegated: kms / hsm delegated mode: completing the switchover is a deployment-level provider migration; follow section 4 of the operations runbook docs/ops/privileged-credential-rotation.md. This page does not give step-by-step instructions.
keyManagement.rotateDataConfirm: This generates a new-generation data encryption key and batch re-encrypts all stored credentials (completes in seconds when the data volume is small; resumable if interrupted). The old key becomes retired and only decrypts existing ciphertext. Rotate?
keyManagement.rotateAuditConfirm: This generates a new-generation audit sealing key: new logs afterward are sealed with the new key, historical logs keep their original seals without recomputation, and verification is unaffected. Rotate?
keyManagement.rotateDataPartial: Rotated to v{version}: {reencrypted} records re-encrypted, {pending} pending (click the rotate button again to resume)
keyManagement.rotateDataDone: Rotation complete: v{from} → v{to}, {reencrypted} records re-encrypted
keyManagement.rotateAuditDone: Sealing key rotation complete: v{from} → v{to}
keyManagement.switchoverDegradedDesc: {n} old KEK row(s) have not completed retirement finalization. Service, connections and encryption/decryption of existing data are entirely unaffected, but the retirement evidence has not converged — restart the backend service so the system re-runs finalization; if it still does not reach zero after a restart, check the backend logs.
keyManagement.switchoverPendingDesc: {n} key row(s) wrapped with the new KEK are awaiting promotion. Store the new KEK in ENCRYPTION_KEY and restart the backend service to complete the switchover.
keyManagement.switchoverPendingDescUi: {n} key row(s) wrapped with the new KEK are awaiting promotion. Restart the backend service, then enter the new KEK on the unseal page to complete the switchover. Do not write the new KEK into .env or ENCRYPTION_KEY.
keyManagement.switchoverPendingDescDelegated: {n} key row(s) wrapped with the new KEK are awaiting promotion. This deployment's KEK is held by a delegated provider, so completing the switchover is a deployment-level provider migration — follow section 4 of the operations runbook docs/ops/privileged-credential-rotation.md.
keyManagement.switchoverPendingDescUnknown: {n} key row(s) wrapped with the new KEK are awaiting promotion. How to complete the switchover depends on this deployment's KEK_PROVIDER (env: write it into ENCRYPTION_KEY and restart; ui: restart and enter it on the unseal page — do not write it into .env; kms / hsm: follow the operations runbook).
keyManagement.cleanupRetiredConfirm: This permanently destroys the key material of retired key rows; fingerprints and retirement history are preserved. Versions still referenced by existing ciphertext or audit signatures are skipped and reported individually.
keyManagement.cleanupRetiredDone: Cleaned up {n} retired key material record(s)
keyManagement.cleanupSkippedVersion: {purpose} v{version}: retained — {refs} stored ciphertexts are encrypted with this version; destroying it would make that data permanently unrecoverable
keyManagement.cleanupSkippedAudit: {purpose} v{version}: retained — {refs} historical audit records are sealed with this key; destroying it would make those records permanently unverifiable (audit requirement, cannot be forced)
keyManagement.cleanupDisabledNotConverged: Key rotation has not fully converged (pending switchover or retirement backlog exists); cleanup is available only after convergence
keyManagement.cleanupDisabledRewrapPending: Cleanup is unavailable while a KEK rewrap awaits switchover; complete or abandon the rewrap first
keyManagement.pubKeyFingerprintLabel: Public key fingerprint (Ed25519 export-signing public key; safe to share)
keyManagement.kekHistoryHint: Retirement records of past KEK switchovers; retired rows are kept permanently for audit and contain no key material
keyManagement.rewrapConflict: Rewrap conflict: {detail} Complete the switch first (store the new KEK into ENCRYPTION_KEY and restart) or abandon this switch, then retry.
keyManagement.switchoverUnknownDesc: Failed to read switchover state (transient database error); the numbers shown are unreliable. Cleanup is conservatively disabled — please refresh later.
keyManagement.cleanupDisabledStateUnknown: Convergence state could not be read; cleanup is disabled while the state is unknown
keyManagement.cleanupConfirmCandidatesTitle: Will attempt to destroy the following retired key rows (same order as the table: most recently retired first; versions still referenced by stored ciphertext or audit records are skipped automatically):
keyManagement.cleanupConfirmKekRows: Additionally, {n} wrapped rows of retired KEKs will be destroyed.
keyManagement.cleanupConfirmRestartNotice: Before cleaning up, make sure every backend instance has been restarted to the latest key state; an instance still writing old-version ciphertext would make data unrecoverable.
keyManagement.cleanupDisabledRotating: A key rotation is in progress; clean up after it finishes
keyManagement.cleanupSkippedUnregistered: {purpose} v{version}: retained — no cleanup rule is defined for this key type, so the system conservatively keeps it. This is a gap in the program definition and cannot be resolved by an administrator
keyManagement.kekErrorFormat: Cannot be decoded into a 32-byte key: enter 32 characters, 64 hexadecimal characters, or base64 that decodes to exactly 32 bytes

instanceGuard.summary: Another application instance may be using the same database. The guard writes events like this to the audit log, but it sends no notification of any kind: this banner is the notification.
instanceGuard.summaryUnreachable: The database connection was lost, so the guard cannot confirm the lock state right now. This is not a sign of a second instance. While the connection is down the audit log may not be writable either, so this banner is the notification.
instanceGuard.boundary: The guard only makes this visible and records it. It does not prevent data problems caused by two instances running at the same time.
instanceGuard.sinceHeld: this instance has held the lock since {time}

detail.loadFailed: Could not load guard details. Refresh to try again.
detail.holderNone: No other session currently holds the lock
detail.fingerprintUnavailable: Holder details are unavailable. This code is a degraded code and is not bound to a specific session.
detail.ackActor: Acknowledged by: an operator via the INSTANCE_GUARD_ACK environment variable. The system cannot identify who set it; that is owned by your change management process.
detail.riskBody: Two instances running at the same time will cause data problems in the key cache, export jobs, recording storage and sealed-period audit records.
detail.nextStepHolder: Confirm the other instance has stopped. This notice clears automatically once this instance acquires the lock; no restart is needed.
detail.nextStepUnreachable: The guard retries the lock at least every half minute. This notice clears within two minutes once the database connection is restored.
detail.nextStepPermanent: Check the application account's database permissions and the reason in the backend log. The guard keeps retrying the lock.
detail.nextStepPeers: Check whether another instance is running. Once it stops, this notice clears within two minutes. An instance started with an acknowledgement code leaves an instance_guard event in the audit log.

oidcProviders.headerDesc: Configure OIDC identity providers so users can sign in with SSO.
oidcProviders.emptyHint: Click "Add Provider" to create the first identity provider configuration.
oidcProviders.localAdminWarningTitle: External login does not replace local administrators: keep at least one administrator who signs in with a local password
oidcProviders.localAdminWarningDesc: While the system is sealed, only local administrator credentials can unseal it. If every administrator moves to external sign-in, nobody can unseal after a key restart.
oidcProviders.localAdminNoneTitle: No local administrator remains: the system can no longer be unsealed
oidcProviders.localAdminNoneDesc: There is no active administrator who signs in with a local password. Once the system seals, nobody can unseal it (only local administrator credentials are accepted while sealed), so a key restart means a permanent management lockout. Create a local administrator account immediately.

oidcProviders.secretRotateWarning: Rotating the secret immediately invalidates existing sign-in credentials and connections; users must sign in again.
oidcProviders.scopesHint: openid is always sent by the system and cannot be removed; only profile and email may be added.
oidcProviders.namePlaceholder: Name shown on the sign-in page, e.g. Azure AD
oidcProviders.issuerMustBeHttps: The issuer must start with https://
oidcProviders.immutableTooltip: Issuer and Client ID are the identity keys of external identities and cannot be changed after creation; create a new provider instead.
oidcProviders.azureMultiTenantWarning: A Microsoft multi-tenant endpoint (common / organizations / consumers) was detected. Such endpoints report an issuer containing a tenant placeholder rather than the actual value, so strict comparison always fails. Use a tenant-specific issuer instead.
oidcProviders.issuerKindColumnTooltip: Dedicated to this organization = this issuer only issues accounts for your organization (e.g. acme.okta.com, an Azure tenant endpoint). Shared across organizations = a public issuer anyone can sign up with (e.g. accounts.google.com). On a shared issuer, an admission rule based on email domain alone is rejected — anyone can register an account on that domain, so it keeps no outsider out.

issuerKindSourceHint.deploy_declared: This issuer is declared dedicated to this organization by the deployment (OIDC_DEDICATED_ISSUERS).
issuerKindSourceHint.builtin_list: This issuer is on the built-in list of providers shared across organizations and cannot be treated as dedicated to this organization.
issuerKindSourceHint.admin_forced: "Always treat as shared across organizations" is enabled on this page.
issuerKindSourceHint.unknown_default: No source declares this issuer as dedicated to this organization, so the system conservatively treats it as shared across organizations. If you did declare it in the deployment configuration, check the spelling and whether every service replica has been restarted.

oidcProviders.admissionColumnTooltip: Re-evaluated on every sign-in, not only the first one. "Auto-provision by rules (JIT)" = an id_token that satisfies the claim rules is admitted and an account is created automatically. "Pre-bound accounts only" = only accounts whose external identity an administrator has already bound can sign in; no account is created.

admissionHint.prebound_only: Only accounts whose external identity an administrator has already bound can sign in; no accounts are created automatically.
admissionHint.jit_with_rules: Users matching all of the rules below get an account created on first sign-in; rules are combined with AND, values within one list with OR.

oidcProviders.preboundSwitchTitle: Switching to "Pre-bound accounts only" changes admission semantics
oidcProviders.preboundSwitchDesc: Already-bound external identities are unaffected and can keep signing in; users who are not yet bound can no longer sign in until an administrator binds them.
oidcProviders.preboundSwitchDescCount: The {count} already-bound external identities are unaffected and can still sign in; users without a binding can no longer sign in and must be bound by an administrator.
oidcProviders.ruleTidHint: Microsoft Entra tenant GUID; press Enter to add, multiple values allowed.
oidcProviders.ruleHdHint: Google Workspace organization domain; the value is protected by the id_token signature.
oidcProviders.ruleEmailDomainHint: Not sufficient on its own to prove organizational membership: verified email is also required, and an issuer shared across organizations additionally needs a tenant or hosted-domain rule.
oidcProviders.ruleEmailVerifiedHint: Only a boolean true value of email_verified in the id_token is accepted.
oidcProviders.ruleListPlaceholder: Type a value and press Enter
oidcProviders.rulesRequired: At least one admission rule is required when auto-provisioning is enabled
oidcProviders.forceShared: Always treat as shared across organizations
oidcProviders.forceSharedHint: When enabled, the stricter rules for issuers shared across organizations always apply (auto-provisioning must include a tenant or hosted-domain condition). This switch can only tighten; it cannot turn a shared issuer into one dedicated to this organization.
oidcProviders.disableConfirm: After disabling "{name}", existing sessions and connections obtained through this provider become invalid immediately, and re-enabling will not restore them. Disable it?
oidcProviders.deleteConfirm: Delete provider "{name}"? It cannot be deleted while user external identities are still linked; disable it instead.
oidcProviders.admissionIssueTitle: Admission rules of provider "{name}" are no longer compliant; automatic provisioning has stopped
oidcProviders.admissionIssueGeneric: The current admission rules do not satisfy the requirements of this issuer ownership, so automatic provisioning has stopped. Please edit this provider's admission rules.

admissionIssue.shared_needs_org_rule: This issuer is shared across organizations: automatic provisioning must include a tenant (tid) or organization domain (hd) condition. An email-domain rule alone would let in anyone holding an account at that provider.
admissionIssue.empty_rule_set: Rule-based automatic provisioning is enabled but no admission rule is set; that is equivalent to opening the system to everyone, so it is refused.
admissionIssue.consumer_tenant: The rules point at the Microsoft consumer tenant, which proves no organizational affiliation and cannot serve as a basis for automatic provisioning.
admissionIssue.email_needs_verified: An email-domain rule must be combined with "require verified email"; otherwise an unverified address can be claimed at will.
admissionIssue.unknown_rule: The rule set contains condition keys the system does not recognize. To avoid treating unknown conditions as effective, the whole rule set is rejected.
admissionIssue.invalid_rules: The admission rules cannot be parsed (malformed or invalid values). Please edit and save this provider again.

oidcProviders.preboundLimitationTitle: What "pre-bound accounts only" does and does not cover
oidcProviders.preboundLimitationDesc: This mode only checks, at sign-in time, whether the external identity is already bound. Accounts deleted or disabled at the identity provider are therefore kept out, but accounts that still exist while the person's organizational affiliation has changed are not covered — someone who has left but whose account is retained, or who moved to another subsidiary or tenant, can still sign in. Revoking their access requires an admin to unbind the identity or disable the account.
oidcProviders.admissionIssueTitleAll: Admission rules of the following providers are no longer compliant; automatic provisioning has stopped: {names}
oidcProviders.admissionIssueMergedDesc: The cause differs per provider — hover the “Non-compliant rules” badge next to the provider name in the table below to see it, then edit that provider’s admission rules.
oidcProviders.loadFailedTitle: Could not load the provider list
oidcProviders.loadFailedDesc: The list below does not reflect the current configuration. Use Refresh to retry; if it keeps failing, check the server and database status.
oidcProviders.emptyLoadFailedTitle: The list could not be loaded
oidcProviders.emptyLoadFailedHint: This does not mean no providers are configured. Use Refresh to retry.

externalIdentities.claimWarningTitle: IdP-reported values are not identities in this system
externalIdentities.claimWarningDesc: "IdP-reported username" and "IdP-reported email" are entirely controlled at the identity provider and can be changed by the user (for example by setting their own preferred_username to admin). Judge who an identity belongs to by the local account and the subject.
externalIdentities.unbindConsequenceTitle: Unbinding signs the user out of every session
externalIdentities.unbindConsequenceDesc: Unbinding any external identity invalidates all of that user's refresh tokens, already-issued access tokens, in-flight protocol connections, read-only monitoring subscriptions and unredeemed capability tokens — including those established through another provider or a local password. The user must sign in again. This is a deliberate trade-off: one extra sign-in beats a missed revocation.

checkpointVerification.headerDesc: Integrity evidence for the audit checkpoint chain: it shows that the operation logs in the database have not been removed or replaced, and lets an external reviewer verify that independently with the public key. This page is read-only, and it also shows the latest results of the system's automatic checking.

degraded.title: Off-box copy not yet enabled (deployment step outstanding)
degraded.why: Checkpoints currently exist only inside this system. Full protection needs a second copy held somewhere this system cannot write to, so that even if the local data and its checkpoints are replaced wholesale (including a rollback of the whole database to an older backup), the outside copy still shows the difference.
degraded.action: To enable: go to System settings → Security policies, and in the log forwarding section enter the address of the external log collector and turn it on. From then on, every new checkpoint is sent out immediately.
degraded.gap: Checkpoints created before it was enabled have no outside copy, and that gap cannot be filled retroactively: the value of outside evidence is that it was sent at the time, so sending it later does not carry the same weight. The practical approach is to treat the moment of enabling as a new baseline. Only records after that point have both local integrity protection and an outside copy to reconcile against; earlier records keep their local integrity protection but cannot prove they were not replaced wholesale. Enabling it does not remove every blind spot either: the boundaries listed further down this page still apply, so read them before forming a conclusion.

These values are themselves outside the protection of the record chain and can be altered by anyone with write access to the database (see boundary R0 below). statusHint.purged_legal: Deleted under the retention policy, and the deletion claim itself passed verification. This is not an anomaly. To check what the deletion was based on, look up the retention period for this kind of data under System settings → Security policies; no further follow-up is needed.
statusHint.purged_invalid: The records are gone, but there is no verified proof of a legitimate deletion. Treat this as a suspected unauthorized deletion: first check the Operation Logs page for a deletion run in that period, then compare this range against the off-box copy (with the off-box copy not enabled this step cannot be done, and that fact belongs in the finding itself). Until it is resolved, this range cannot be used as audit evidence.
statusHint.count_mismatch: The number of records present differs from the number signed at sealing time. The missing part has to be followed up: check whether a deletion run took place in that period, then compare against the off-box copy to identify which records are missing. Until that is resolved, the count for this range cannot be used as an audit basis.
statusHint.hash_mismatch: The count matches, but the recomputed check value does not match the one signed at sealing time, so content, ordering or key version was altered. Compare this range record by record against the off-box copy to identify which record changed and how. Until that is resolved, the content of this range cannot be used as an audit basis.
statusHint.extra_rows_valid_hmac: This range contains records that were not counted at sealing time, each carrying a valid integrity signature. They may come from a long transaction written after the sealing point, or they may have been inserted afterwards by a holder of the signing key. A person has to judge which (see boundary R1 below). What to weigh: extra records clustered around the sealing point that match work still running at the time are more likely to be late arrivals; records far from that point, or matching no such work, should be treated as inserted after the fact and escalated.
statusHint.signature_invalid: The signature of this checkpoint itself does not verify, so nothing it claims can be trusted. Do not draw conclusions about the range from it: bound what is trustworthy using the nearest checkpoints on either side that still verify, check whether the signing key was replaced or the system rebuilt in that period, and compare against the off-box copy.
statusHint.chain_broken: The link value to the previous checkpoint, or the adjoining of their ranges, does not match. The period between those two checkpoints is the suspect window: check whether a system restore or a database rollback happened then, and compare that range against the off-box copy.
statusHint.seq_gap: The numbering is not continuous and no matching record of a legitimate deletion under the retention policy exists. Check whether a retention deletion ran over the missing stretch; if no such record exists, treat the checkpoint as removed and reconcile that stretch against the off-box copy.

limits.title: What this mechanism protects, and where its boundaries are
limits.intro: Below is each situation this mechanism cannot prevent, together with the control that carries that risk instead. Listing boundaries does not mean the overall control fails; it defines what this mechanism proves. Any assurance beyond that scope does not hold.

protection.P1: At regular intervals the system seals the existing operation log records and signs them, producing a checkpoint. If sealed records are later modified, deleted or inserted, verification can point to the stretch where it happened, rather than only reporting that something is wrong. This mechanism covers the operation logs, and the file transfer records that the Investigation Workbench lists separately are held in the operation logs too, so they are covered as well. Other sources such as command streams, alert records and connection recordings are not included.
protection.P2: The signing key is held separately from the database, so someone who holds database access alone — a database administrator, say, or an intruder who gets no further than the database — cannot produce records that pass verification, even with the ability to write or alter rows. That is the whole of this claim: it does not extend to anyone who holds the signing key and the database together. That case is boundary R0 below, and this mechanism does not prevent it.
protection.P3: An external reviewer can verify independently with the public key shown on this page, without trusting this system or any tool we supply. The encoding specification and a standalone verification tool are published.
protection.P4: Nobody has to remember to run these checks. After every sealing the system re-checks the stretches sealed within a recent period, and on a configured interval it works through the whole history in turn, opening a Failure Events entry and sending an alert if a notification channel is configured. What the automatic checking can detect is exactly what you get by running the checks on this page by hand: what it shortens is the time between tampering and discovery, not the range of what can be detected. How it is currently running is shown near the top of this page.

limits.boundaryTitle: Boundaries, and what carries each risk

R0.scenario: Someone who holds both the signing key and the database (a top-level administrator, for example, or anyone able to run arbitrary programs on the server) could in principle rebuild the entire record chain, and could also falsely claim that certain records were legitimately deleted under the retention policy.
R0.mitigation: Carried by the off-box copy, which is the only counter: every checkpoint is sent to an independent log collector as it is created, so a forged chain will not match what the collector retained, and going unnoticed would mean controlling this system and the collector at the same time. This defense has limits of its own and should not be recorded as a dual-authorization control: the collector may not be configured at all (see R3), and checkpoints are sent without waiting for acknowledgment, so the status on this page is never revised (see R4). Judge the strength of this control by what the collector actually retained, not by the status shown here.

R1.scenario: A very long transaction may write its records into the database only after that stretch has been sealed, in which case verification flags them as extra records.
R1.mitigation: Each of those records still carries its own integrity signature. The system marks them for human review, neither declaring them tampering nor letting them through silently: between a false alarm and a missed one, it chooses honest marking.

R2.scenario: When the database is unavailable, records are written to a fallback file instead, and at write peaks a full internal buffer can also mean a whole batch never reaches the database. Records in either situation are outside the coverage of this mechanism.
R2.mitigation: Both situations leave an entry on the Failure Events tab of the Operation Logs page, and an alert is sent out when a notification channel is configured, so when it happened and how long it lasted can be traced. Those entries are held separately, however, and are not covered by the sealing and signing of this mechanism; how far they can be trusted depends on database access control. What this mechanism proves is that the records in the operation logs were not touched, which is not the same as proving that every event reached the operation logs.

R3.scenario: With no external log collector configured, this mechanism covers local integrity only and cannot counter replacing the local data together with its checkpoints wholesale, including a rollback of the whole database to an older backup.
R3.mitigation: The only thing carrying this today is the prompt inside the product: while it is unconfigured, the top of this page states plainly that the system is in a degraded state and points to the log forwarding settings under System settings → Security policies, so no claim of full protection is made from an unconfigured state. There is, however, no pre-deployment checklist that makes an external log collector a required companion control, so whether the collector is configured depends on whether the deploying party read that prompt and followed it.

R4.scenario: Checkpoints are sent to the collector without waiting for a reply, so there is no acknowledgment of receipt, and individual events can be lost during network trouble or traffic peaks.
R4.mitigation: The off-box status shown on this page only means the checkpoint was handed over locally for sending; it is not a confirmation of receipt by the collector. Once handed over, the status is never revised, whether sending then fails locally, forwarding is turned off and the item is discarded, or the item is lost on the network after being sent. An entry is written to the Failure Events tab of the Operation Logs page when an item is discarded before it is handed over, but a run of consecutive discards raises only one; and if the process stops between writing the checkpoint and handing it over, the status stays at not sent with no matching alert. Complete proof is local chain verification together with a comparison against what the collector retained; the two corroborate each other.

R5.scenario: Records created after the most recent sealing are not yet covered by the chain{window}. If a record in that stretch is deleted outright, sealing captures the state after the deletion, and it cannot be discovered afterwards from local data.
R5.mitigation: The content of records in that stretch is still protected by their own integrity signatures, so edits to content remain detectable. Outright deletion has to be caught by the off-box copy, since the record was sent out before it was deleted. An administrator can shorten the sealing interval to narrow this stretch. The automatic checking shortens the time between tampering and discovery for sealed stretches only; it does not cover the not-yet-sealed stretch described here. The recent period used by the check after each sealing refers to sealing time, so records not yet sealed are never part of it.

R6.scenario: The response status code and the processing duration are two fields outside the signature coverage, so changes to them cannot be detected.
R6.mitigation: Neither field is used as a basis for an audit finding. The four core fields, who acted, when, on which asset and what action, are all protected, and the key version field is covered as well — it has been since the first checkpoint listed on this page, so there is no earlier stretch left outside the coverage.

limit.scope_is_query_range: The report covers the whole query range, not just the rows currently loaded on screen.
limit.truncated_differs: The load limit on screen and the per-category limit in the report are different things; the report records both separately and never merges them.
limit.csv_formula_escape: Text cells in the CSV files that start with = + - {'@'} Tab or CR get a leading apostrophe so spreadsheets do not run them as formulas; plain numbers are left as they are. For the exact original text, look the record up in the system by its record reference.
limit.payload_excluded: The report contains event facts only — no clipboard text, no transferred file, no recording — and the reasons differ. Clipboard text is still held in the system and simply is not exported with the report; when you need the content itself there are two routes — reveal it entry by entry on the session detail page, or request an evidence bundle instead, which carries the decrypted text in full. Both routes are themselves recorded. A transferred file is never held by this system at all: only its name, path, size and content fingerprint are recorded, so the file itself cannot be obtained at any time. Recordings are not exported with the report either; whether a session has one is stated row by row through the recording status, and the footage itself likewise comes from an evidence bundle.
limit.coverage_states: Where records for a period were deleted under the retention policy, the report marks that period, and where checkpoints cover that stretch it states their number range as well — a blank stretch does not mean nothing happened.
limit.coverage_states_detail: Categories that are never deleted automatically (sessions and clipboard, for example) are not removed by the retention policy, so a blank stretch there was not caused by deletion. It still does not mean nothing happened: only events the system actually captures become records. Clipboard events, for instance, are captured only on graphical desktop sessions and only for text — terminal sessions and database sessions never produce a clipboard record.
limit.recording_state: Recording status is inferred from deletion progress by time, not verified file by file; 'no recording' means the session has no recording at all, which is different from 'deleted under the retention policy'.
limit.manifest_required: Completeness rule: if the report has no manifest file, the export failed part-way and the package is incomplete — it must not be used as evidence.
limit.no_offline_tool: The report does not bundle an offline verification tool, and the standalone verifier for the checkpoint chain does not cover this report either. To verify a report yourself, the technical documentation shipped with this system sets out how to obtain the verification key and the exact steps for checking the signature; ask the system administrator for a copy.
limit.not_signed: Report signing is not enabled on this system (reason code {reason}), so this report has no signature file. Signing was never turned on here; the file was not removed after the fact.
limit.asset_scope: For an asset, operation records cover only entries that carry an asset association; that association has only been recorded since the Investigation Workbench went live on this system, so earlier operation records will not appear in an asset-scoped result. The date depends on when this deployment was upgraded, so ask the system administrator for the upgrade record when your working papers have to state the period the evidence covers.
limit.bundle_plaintext: This bundle contains clipboard text in the clear and the session recordings themselves, all of it confidential. What the system can guarantee is that the handover is recorded; once collected, safekeeping is the recipient's responsibility.
limit.bundle_async: An evidence bundle does not download immediately: packaging runs in the background and the file can only be collected once it completes. Artifacts are kept for a limited time; after that they are deleted automatically and the download address stops working.
limit.bundle_requester_only: Only the person who requested it can download this artifact; other accounts are refused even when they hold audit view permission. Anyone who needs the same data should request their own copy, so every copy records who collected it.
limit.bundle_category_scope: This bundle collects only the categories you selected; an unselected category is left out entirely and its counts are absent from the manifest (writing a zero would make "not selected" look like "none in scope"). Alerts and file transfers have no content of their own and are included as fact lists.
limit.bundle_clipboard_gap: If clipboard content failed to encrypt at capture time, that entry is marked in the bundle as a retention failure with the content field absent — it is never faked with an empty string. That is a gap, not an empty clipboard.
limit.bundle_scope_is_query_range: What is collected is the whole query range, not just the records already loaded on screen.
limit.bundle_truncated_differs: The on-screen load limit and the per-category limit inside the bundle are two different things; the manifest records them separately and never merges them.
limit.bundle_manifest_required: Completeness test: if the package contains no manifest, packaging failed midway, that copy is incomplete and must not be used as evidence.
limit.bundle_no_offline_tool: No offline verification tool ships inside the package. To verify this bundle yourself, how to obtain the verification key and the step-by-step verification commands are in this system's external technical documentation; ask your administrator for it.

ipBoundary.candidates: Candidates cover only addresses that have signed in or connected successfully. An address that appears only in denial records has no candidate entry, but can be typed in directly — that is what free input is for.
ipBoundary.scope: Connections, activity logs and file transfers carry their own address field. Commands, alerts and clipboard records do not — what you see is the source their parent connection was established from, as stated on each address cell.
ipBoundary.unknown: Records with no retrievable source show as "Unknown" with a reason (system-initiated, unresolvable at write time, or parent connection gone). Records with neither an attributable user nor an address cannot be reached from any pivot — that limit is stated here and nowhere else.
ipBoundary.ipv6: Temporary IPv6 addresses rotate, so one device appears here as several addresses; the system does not aggregate prefixes. Correlating them is up to the investigator, using time and account.
ipBoundary.proxy: When the deployment has not declared a trusted proxy chain, every record shows the proxy address. That is a deployment setting, owned by the operator and the deployment documentation; it affects all records at once, so no per-row marker is possible.
ipBoundary.export: Export is not available on the source address pivot. Switch to the user or asset pivot to produce a report — the source address column in those reports is unchanged.
ipBoundary.exactMatch: Addresses are matched exactly after normalization. Range and prefix queries are not supported.
